case_name: Dinesh Shankarnarayan Kumarkandath vs The State Of Maharashtra And Another

parties.petitioner_plaintiff: Dinesh Shankarnarayan Kumarkandath, husband; Shankarnarayan Kumarkandath Nair, father-in-law; Vatsala Shankarnarayan Kumarkandath Nair, mother-in-law; Ganesh Shankarnarayan Kumarkandth Nair, brother-in-law; Maya Ganesh Nair, sister-in-law
parties.respondent_defendant: The State of Maharashtra, respondent No.1; Veena Dinesh Nair, respondent No.2

facts_of_case: Parties have arrived at amicable settlement and seeking quashing of proceedings bearing R.C.C. No. 1906/2022 pending before the Judicial Magistrate, First Class, Aurangabad arising out of Crime No. 177/2020 registered with Satara Police Station for the offences punishable under Sections 498-A, 323, 505, 506 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code.

legal_principles.principle: The power to quash a criminal proceeding or FIR or complaint in exercise of its inherent jurisdiction is distinct and different from the power given to a criminal court for compounding the offences under Section 320 of the Code.
legal_principles.held: The position that emerges from the above discussion can be summarised thus: the power of the High Court in quashing a criminal proceeding or FIR or complaint in exercise of its inherent jurisdiction is distinct and different from the power given to a criminal court for compounding the offences under Section 320 of the Code.
cited_cases: Gian Singh vs. State of Punjab and others, (2012) 10 SCC 303
Kulwinder Singh v. State of Punjab (2007) 4 CTC 769

legal_principles.principle: The power to quash a criminal proceeding or FIR or complaint may be exercised where the offender and the victim have settled their dispute, but this depends on the facts and circumstances of each case.
legal_principles.held: In what cases power to quash the criminal proceeding or complaint or FIR may be exercised where the offender and the victim have settled their dispute would depend on the facts and circumstances of each case and no category can be prescribed.
cited_cases: Gian Singh vs. State of Punjab and others, (2012) 10 SCC 303
Kulwinder Singh v. State of Punjab (2007) 4 CTC 769

legal_principles.principle: Heinous and serious offences of mental depravity or offences like murder, rape, dacoity, etc. cannot be fittingly quashed even though the victim or victim's family and the offender have settled the dispute.
legal_principles.held: Such offences are not private in nature.
cited_cases: Gian Singh vs. State of Punjab and others, (2012) 10 SCC 303
Kulwinder Singh v. State of Punjab (2007) 4 CTC 769

legal_principles.principle: Before exercising the power to quash a criminal proceeding or FIR or complaint, the High Court must have due regard to the nature and gravity of the crime.
legal_principles.held: However, before exercise of such power, the High Court must have due regard to the nature and gravity of the crime.
cited_cases: Gian Singh vs. State of Punjab and others, (2012) 10 SCC 303
Kulwinder Singh v. State of Punjab (2007) 4 CTC 769
keywords: nature and gravity of the crime

outcome.final_order: Petitioners' prayer for quashing of proceedings bearing R.C.C. No. 1906/2022 is allowed.
